entries.content: After handling fulfillment disputes for 3 years, I've noticed empty box claims tend to cluster. When you see multiple similar claims in a short window, it's usually coordinated—word spreads in buyer communities about which excuses work. Our team started requiring unboxing video proof for any empty box claim when we're seeing elevated volumes, and our dispute losses dropped significantly. The legitimate customers understand and comply quickly.

Root cause analysis on September's empty package spike: 73% traced to Warehouse B's new tape gun malfunction causing seal failures during transit. Remaining cases distributed across normal variance. Carrier liability claims filed for 12 confirmed theft incidents on Route 7.

When you're seeing a pattern of similar claims, it makes sense to apply additional verification. Customers making legitimate claims typically have no issue providing documentation like photos of the packaging or a brief video showing the condition upon arrival. You can frame it as helping expedite their case. If they push back strongly on providing any evidence, that reaction itself is informative for your assessment.

Empty package claims represent a known vector for refund abuse. Industry data shows that when multiple empty package claims originate from similar demographics or timeframes, the probability of coordinated abuse increases substantially. Experienced support teams often implement tiered verification—requesting unboxing documentation for claims fitting higher-risk profiles—to balance customer service with loss prevention.

Compliance flagged two chargebacks from Q4 where we denied refunds citing 'pattern of similar claims' without individual case investigation. Both ruled in customer favor. Payment processor warned that pattern-based denials without case-specific evidence create liability exposure.
